rows.stem: Which part of the ovule hardens to form seed coat of a seed ?
rows.solution: After fertilisation the ovule develops into the seed. In this change the **integuments of the ovule harden into the tough protective seed coat** (the outer testa and inner tegmen), the zygote gives rise to the embryo and the primary endosperm nucleus to the endosperm. The micropyle remains as a small pore in the seed coat. The funicle is only the stalk that attaches the ovule to the placenta, the chalaza is the basal region of the ovule, and the nucellus is the mass of tissue inside the integuments that is usually used up. So the answer is option (D) Integuments.

rows.stem:
Consider the following statements and choose the correct option :
Statement I : Using vaccination and immunization programmes, we have been able to eradicate smallpox.
Statement II : Vaccines are available for diphtheria and polio.

options.label: A
options.text: Both Statements I and II are false.

options.label: B
options.text: Both Statements I and II are true.

rows.solution:
- Statement I is true: **vaccination and immunisation programmes have enabled us to completely eradicate smallpox**, a deadly disease.
- Statement II is true: vaccines are available against several infectious diseases, and through immunisation diseases such as **polio, diphtheria, pneumonia and tetanus** have been controlled to a large extent.

So the answer is option (B) Both Statements I and II are true.

rows.stem: Taylor and colleagues performed an experiment on which of the following organisms to provide proof for semi-conservative replication of DNA in chromosomes ?
rows.solution: In 1958, **Taylor and colleagues** used **Vicia faba (faba beans)** and radioactive thymidine to detect the distribution of newly synthesised DNA in the chromosomes, and showed that DNA in chromosomes also replicates **semi-conservatively**. The same mode had been proved earlier in Escherichia coli by Meselson and Stahl, using heavy nitrogen (\(^{15}\text{N}\)). So the answer is option (C) Vicia faba.

rows.stem: Which cells are responsible for producing antibodies in a human body ?
rows.solution: Antibodies are produced by the **B-lymphocytes**: in response to a pathogen entering the body, they produce an army of proteins called antibodies into the blood (the humoral immune response). The T-lymphocytes do not secrete antibodies themselves; helper T cells help the B cells to produce them, and cytotoxic T cells kill infected cells directly (cell-mediated immunity). Macrophages are phagocytic cells of the innate immunity. So the answer is option (D) B-Lymphocytes.

rows.stem: Which of the following is a secondary consumer ?
rows.solution: A **secondary consumer** is a carnivore that feeds on herbivores (the primary consumers), and it occupies the **third trophic level**. In an aquatic food chain, phytoplankton (producers) are eaten by zooplankton (primary consumers), which in turn are eaten by **fish**, so the fish is a secondary consumer. The grasshopper and the cow feed on plants and are primary consumers, while the hawk is a top carnivore that feeds on other carnivores such as snakes. So the answer is option (C) Fish.

rows.stem: The method of contraception that is hormone-based and prevents ovulation is :
rows.solution: **Oral pills** are tablets of **progestogens or progestogen-estrogen combinations** taken daily. Being hormonal, they **inhibit ovulation** and implantation and alter the quality of the cervical mucus to prevent the entry of sperms. Copper-T and Lippes loop are intra-uterine devices (the Lippes loop is non-medicated and Copper-T releases copper ions that suppress sperm motility), and the condom is a barrier method; none of these stops ovulation. So the answer is option (A) Oral Pills.

rows.stem:
Assertion (A) : Hardy-Weinberg principle says that allele frequencies in a population are stable.
Reason (R) : Hardy-Weinberg principle is applicable only when genetic drift does not occur.
rows.context: For Questions number 13 to 16, two statements are given – one labelled as Assertion (A) and the other labelled as Reason (R). Select the correct answer to these questions from the codes (A), (B), (C) and (D) as given below.

options.label: A
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: C
options.text: Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.

options.label: D
options.text: Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.

rows.solution:
The Assertion is true: the **Hardy-Weinberg principle** says that allele frequencies in a population are stable and constant from generation to generation, so the gene pool (the total genes and their alleles in a population) remains constant. This is called genetic equilibrium, and the sum of the allelic frequencies is 1 (\(p^2 + 2pq + q^2 = 1\)).

The Reason is false: the equilibrium holds only when **none** of the factors that change allele frequencies is operating. There are five such factors: **gene migration or gene flow, genetic drift, mutation, genetic recombination and natural selection**. Absence of genetic drift alone is therefore not enough for the principle to apply.

So the Assertion is true while the Reason is false, which is option (C).

rows.stem:
A patient reports a high fever, chills and sweating. His blood shows the presence of a toxic substance.
(i) Identify the disease and the causative organism.
(ii) Explain why this disease shows recurring pattern of fever.
rows.solution:
(i) The disease is **malaria**. It is caused by **Plasmodium**, a protozoan; different species are responsible for different types of malaria: Plasmodium vivax, Plasmodium malariae and Plasmodium falciparum (any one). Plasmodium enters the human body as sporozoites through the bite of an infected female Anopheles mosquito.

(ii) The parasites first multiply in the liver cells and then attack the **red blood cells (RBCs)**, multiplying inside them and causing their rupture. The rupture of RBCs is associated with the release of a toxic substance, **haemozoin**, which is responsible for the **chill and high fever recurring every three to four days**. The fever recurs because each cycle of multiplication inside the RBCs ends in a fresh round of rupture and a fresh release of haemozoin.

rows.stem:
Give the microbial source and mode of action of the following bioactive molecules :
(i) Cyclosporin-A
(ii) Streptokinase
rows.solution:
(i) **Cyclosporin A**
- Microbial source: the fungus **Trichoderma polysporum**.
- Mode of action: it is used as an **immunosuppressive agent in organ-transplant patients**, so that the body does not reject the transplanted organ.

(ii) **Streptokinase**
- Microbial source: the bacterium **Streptococcus** (and modified by genetic engineering).
- Mode of action: it is used as a **"clot buster"** for removing clots from the blood vessels of patients who have undergone myocardial infarction leading to heart attack.

rows.stem: State any four reasons why Mendel succeeded in his genetic hybridisation experiments on garden peas.
rows.solution:
Mendel succeeded in his hybridisation experiments on garden peas for these reasons (any four):
- He applied **statistical analysis and mathematical logic** to problems in biology for the first time.
- He used a **large sampling size**, which gave greater credibility to the data he collected.
- His experiments were carried out over **successive generations** of his test plants, and the confirmation of his inferences proved that his results pointed to **general rules of inheritance** rather than being unsubstantiated ideas.
- He chose characters that were manifested as **two opposing (contrasting) traits**, for example tall or dwarf plants and round or wrinkled seeds, and selected **14 true-breeding pea plant varieties** as pairs that were similar except for one character.
- The garden pea itself was a suitable plant: it has many visible contrasting characters, and its flowers can be artificially cross-pollinated or allowed to self-pollinate.

rows.stem:
A foreign company patented the medicinal use of turmeric already known to Indian households.
(a) Name and define this unethical practice.
(b) What has the Indian Government done to check this ?
rows.solution:
(a) The practice is **biopiracy**. Biopiracy is the term used to refer to the **use of bio-resources (and traditional knowledge) by multinational companies and other organisations without proper authorisation from the countries and people concerned, and without compensatory payment**. Patenting the medicinal use of turmeric, already known to Indian households, is an example.

(b) To check such unauthorised exploitation, the **Indian Parliament has cleared the second amendment of the Indian Patents Bill**, which takes these issues into consideration, including patent terms, emergency provisions and research and development initiatives.

rows.stem:
(a) Who discovered Penicillin and how ? Explain.
(b) Why is this discovery considered accidental ?
(c) In what way did it prove to be a 'milestone' in the field of medicine ?
rows.solution:
(a) Penicillin was discovered by **Alexander Fleming**. While working on **Staphylococci bacteria**, he observed that a **mould had grown in one of his unwashed culture plates**, and that around the mould the Staphylococci could not grow (the bacterial colonies there were killed). He found that this was due to a **chemical produced by the mould**, and he named it **Penicillin** after the mould **Penicillium notatum**.

(b) The discovery is considered **accidental** because it was a **chance observation**: Fleming had not set out to look for an antibacterial substance, and the mould had grown by chance on a culture plate left unwashed.

(c) Penicillin was the **first antibiotic**, and its discovery marked the **beginning of the antibiotic era**. Its full potential as an effective antibiotic was established later by Ernest Chain and Howard Florey, and it was used extensively to **treat soldiers wounded in World War II**. Fleming, Chain and Florey were awarded the Nobel Prize in 1945. Antibiotics have since greatly improved our capacity to treat deadly diseases such as plague, whooping cough, diphtheria and leprosy.

rows.stem:
The following questions are based on the classic experiment conducted by Hershey and Chase.
(i) Why were bacteriophages chosen by the scientists ?
(ii) Name the radioactive isotopes used and state the reason for using them.
(iii) Describe the steps of the experiment.
(iv) Why is this experiment considered a major breakthrough in the field of molecular biology ?
rows.solution:
(i) Bacteriophages were chosen because:
- a bacteriophage is made of **only two components, DNA and protein**, so the experiment could decide which of the two is the genetic material;
- it infects bacteria (E. coli) by **injecting its genetic material** into the cell, while the protein coat stays outside, so the two parts can be followed separately.

(ii) Two radioactive isotopes were used:
- **radioactive phosphorus, \(^{32}\text{P}\)**: some viruses were grown on a medium containing it, because phosphorus is present in **DNA but not in proteins**, so it labels only the DNA;
- **radioactive sulphur, \(^{35}\text{S}\)**: other viruses were grown on a medium containing it, because sulphur is present in **proteins but not in DNA**, so it labels only the protein coat.

(iii) Steps of the experiment (Hershey and Chase, 1952):
- **Infection**: the radioactive phages were allowed to attach to E. coli bacteria and infect them.
- **Blending**: as the infection proceeded, the viral coats were removed from the bacteria by agitating them in a blender.
- **Centrifugation**: the virus particles were separated from the bacteria by spinning them in a centrifuge; the bacteria settle at the bottom and the lighter viral coats stay in the supernatant.

Result: bacteria infected with viruses carrying **radioactive DNA were radioactive**, showing that DNA was the material that passed from the virus into the bacteria. Bacteria infected with viruses carrying **radioactive proteins were not radioactive**, showing that proteins did not enter the bacteria from the virus.

(iv) The experiment is considered a major breakthrough because it gave **unequivocal proof that DNA, and not protein, is the genetic material** that passes from the virus to the bacteria. It settled the long debate over whether protein or DNA carries hereditary information, and laid the foundation for later work on the structure and function of DNA.

rows.stem:
(i) What are multiple alleles ? How do they differ from simple dominant-recessive allele pairs ?
(ii) Explain the concept of multiple alleles with the help of a human trait studied by you.
(iii) Mention all possible genotypes with their corresponding phenotypes of the human trait as explained by you.
(iv) Comment on the type of inheritance pattern involved in the example explained by you.
rows.solution:
(i) **Multiple alleles**: when **more than two alternative forms (alleles) of a gene govern the same character** in a population, they are called multiple alleles.
- In simple dominant-recessive inheritance a gene has only **two alleles**, one dominant and one recessive.
- In multiple allelism the gene has **three or more alleles** in the population, although any one diploid individual can carry only two of them. Multiple alleles can therefore be found only when population studies are made.

(ii) The **ABO blood groups** in humans are an example. They are controlled by the gene **I**, which has **three alleles**: \(\text{I}^{\text{A}}\), \(\text{I}^{\text{B}}\) and i. The plasma membrane of the red blood cells carries sugar polymers whose kind is controlled by this gene: \(\text{I}^{\text{A}}\) and \(\text{I}^{\text{B}}\) each produce a slightly different form of the sugar, while i produces none. Since humans are diploid, each person carries any two of the three alleles.

(iii) The possible genotypes and their blood group phenotypes are six genotypes giving four phenotypes:

| Blood group (phenotype) | Genotype |
|---|---|
| A | \(\text{I}^{\text{A}}\text{I}^{\text{A}}\) or \(\text{I}^{\text{A}}\text{i}\) |
| B | \(\text{I}^{\text{B}}\text{I}^{\text{B}}\) or \(\text{I}^{\text{B}}\text{i}\) |
| AB | \(\text{I}^{\text{A}}\text{I}^{\text{B}}\) |
| O | ii |

(iv) The alleles \(\text{I}^{\text{A}}\) and \(\text{I}^{\text{B}}\) are each **completely dominant over i**. But when \(\text{I}^{\text{A}}\) and \(\text{I}^{\text{B}}\) are present together, both express themselves and the person has the **AB blood group**, carrying both types of sugar. This is **co-dominance**. So ABO blood grouping shows multiple allelism together with co-dominance (and dominance of \(\text{I}^{\text{A}}\) and \(\text{I}^{\text{B}}\) over i).
